web_title: 0. Executive Thesis, Dual Verdict & Opportunity Matrix
book_title: Prologue: The Business, The Price & Our Independent Verdict
title: A Good Franchise, Priced for Perfection
question: What does Xpro India do, what is it worth against the price, and what should you do with new money and with any existing holding?

epigraph.quote: “...we believe this is a short-lived interruption in a long-term journey.”
epigraph.author: Xpro India investor release, 6 November 2025, on the delayed Barjora dielectric line [1]

web_blocks.html: Xpro India makes two very different things. At Barjora in West Bengal it makes polypropylene dielectric (capacitor) film. This is a micron-thin specialty film. It goes inside the capacitors of fans, refrigerators, solar and wind inverters and electric-vehicle drives. At Greater Noida and Ranjangaon it makes plain coextruded plastic sheet, thermoformed refrigerator liners and cast film. In FY2026 revenue was ₹505.5 Cr. Dielectric film was 26.8% of it and the Coex businesses about 73%. Xpro reports one segment, so profit by division is not disclosed [2]. Since 2024 it has committed roughly ₹700 Cr to two new dielectric lines. One is at Barjora, with commercial production declared on 27 March 2026. The other is in the UAE, guided for commercial operation by March 2027. Together they would raise capacity from 4,000 t to 13,000 t [2][3].

New-capital verdict: REJECTED. The 12 November 2026 close was ₹1,142.20. Market capitalisation is ₹2,681 Cr. The shares trade at 76.0x trailing earnings and 3.46x book value. The company earned a 3.8% ROCE in its latest year [4][5]. Our probability-weighted value is ₹865 a share, 24.3% below the close. The bear case is ₹414, the base case ₹811 and the bull case ₹1,674. The business is not the objection. Pass 1 rated it CYCLICAL_CONDITIONAL with KPI health PASS_WITH_WATCH, which means a real but unproven franchise. The price is the objection. It already pays for a full ramp of both new lines. Management has delivered late every time it has set a date.

Current holding action: NOT_HELD. The same-session positions ledger shows no XPROINDIA shares among its 18 Zerodha positions. There is nothing to keep, trim or exit. Zero shares are to be sold, and no stop applies. Redeployment: the next marginal cash unit stays 100% in cash, 0% in the active shortlist and 0% in outside candidates. This run underwrote no alternative to the same standard.

Bull versus bear in one breath. The bull points to Indian import dependence of about 70%. Q2 FY2027 revenue rose 47.4% with dielectric up 64%. The new line turned EBITDA-positive in October 2026. Net debt is ₹40.3 Cr before leases. If management's own ranges hold, profit is about ₹106 Cr and the market capitalisation is 25.3x that [3][6]. The bear points to a 76x multiple on a business whose return on capital fell from 20.7% to 3.4%. The implied dielectric margin is 16-23% against the 35-55% quoted. About 22,500 t of Indian capacity chases about 15,000 t of demand. Every start-up date has slipped, by 6 to 21 months, and one unnamed customer is 29.6% of revenue [2][7]. Weighted honestly, the bear wins at this price.

web_blocks.takeaway: A good business at a price that leaves no room for the usual slippage is a reject, not a wait.

web_blocks.html: What changes the answer. One route is a price in ₹620-660, where our base case clears 1.5:1. Another is evidence that the central case is being beaten. That means Barjora Line 2 at 70-80% utilisation in the March 2027 quarter, the UAE line capitalised and a disclosed dielectric margin above 30%, together with a price near ₹1,020 or lower. A third is a weekly close above ₹1,200 on weekly volume of at least 1.5x the average week. That would repair the chart but not the valuation [3].

book_paragraphs: Before we dive into the chapters, let me give you the whole story in one sitting, the way I would at the start of a long lunch. Xpro India is a Birla-family company that makes two things you will never see on a shelf. One is a hair-thin plastic film that goes inside the capacitors that smooth the electricity in your fan, your refrigerator, a solar inverter or an electric car. The other is ordinary plastic sheet that gets heated and pressed into the inside walls of refrigerators. Most people hear 'plastic film' and imagine snack packaging, and the Managing Director goes out of his way to say it is not that [9].

Why does a company like this deserve a ten-chapter study? Because it is in the middle of a bet. Between 2024 and 2027 it is spending roughly ₹700 Cr, more than its entire annual revenue of ₹505.5 Cr, to build two new film lines and take capacity from 4,000 tonnes to 13,000 [2][3]. If the bet works, it becomes India's scarce supplier of a product the country mostly imports. If it does not, shareholders own a plain-plastic business with a very large depreciation bill.

Here is where I come out, and I want to be plain about it. My verdict for new money is REJECTED. Please hear what that does and does not mean. The business is real: clean audits, an A-/A1 credit rating, repaid banks, a franchise customers had to qualify before buying. But on the 12 November close of ₹1,142.20 the stock sits at 76 times last year's earnings and 3.5 times book value, for a company that earned 3.8% on its capital in the latest year. When I weighed three possible futures, the average came to ₹865 a share, about 24% below the price [4].

The two sides deserve their strongest arguments. The bull says: revenue rose 47% in the September quarter, the new line is making money, India imports 70% of this film, and if management simply meets its own targets the company is worth today's price at only 25 times profit. The bear says: you are paying for that success before it arrives, the company has been late with every new line, there is about 50% more Indian capacity coming than the country needs, and the return on capital has fallen from 21% to 3% while the spending went up. Notice that both are describing the same facts. They differ on the price you should pay for the uncertainty.

You may be wondering what you should do with that. If you do not own the stock, nothing; the ledger confirms there are no Xpro shares in your account, so no selling and no stop to set. Keep the next spare rupee in cash. If you want to revisit, I have written the conditions down: a price around ₹620 to ₹660, where my numbers would offer one and a half times as much reward as risk with a stop at ₹560, or proof that the new lines are filling at a profitable margin, ideally with the price nearer ₹1,020 than ₹1,140.

One last thing, about honesty. The chart has bounced hard from its March low and a 13 November print of ₹1,190.10 looked better still, but it came on thin volume and just under a flat 30-week average, so I would not treat it as a signal [10]. I held myself to one rule throughout: judge the business first, without looking at the price, and only then ask whether the price is fair. Chapters 1 to 6 were written blind. Chapters 7 to 9 are where the price enters.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: The hardest sentence in investing is 'good company, wrong price'. It feels like a contradiction until you see that a price is a promise about the future, and this one is a promise that nothing will slip. Keep the verdict and the business quality in separate boxes, and you can respect one while declining the other.
